inline.s: Two old men, ill, lean on a staff; a boy pounds medicine
If this body were not, where could sickness rise? / The remedy for it—I know not its name.
Three: holding the ruyi scepter, sitting calm and at ease
He holds the ruyi; the ruyi burdens his hand. / Silently he looks within—what is there, after all?
Four: lifting the bowl and reaching into space, as if to take something
Nothing was there to begin with; in emptiness he seeks in vain. / Seeking what cannot be found, is he not ashamed?
Five and six: old men so gaunt they seem too frail for their robes, leaning on a youth who drags them along
Old and thin, too weak to walk; he should rest. / Why burden the boy, who tugs and strains?
Seven: holding pattra leaves, walking fast, looking back at the old man as if waiting for something
Walking alone is quick and easy, yet he frets for another. / The pattra leaves in his hand were nearly dropped.
Eight and nine: old men going ahead on staves, a boy carrying incense behind them as an offering, a ghost nearby in a posture of refuge
His steps are hard; his reliance is the boy. / This one stick of incense is not for the mountain ghost.
Ten: flying through the air on his staff, startling the mountain god; the Elder walks slowly, turning his head to look back
His staff flies up through empty space; the mountain god starts up. / Stay a while, Master—the Dharma banner stands here.
Eleven: Taming the Dragon
Because the dragon's nature is fierce, the Master showed his rougher art; / he only tames its nature—he does not take its pearl.
Twelve: Old and strengthless, his hand resting on a lone pine
A lifetime of pilgrimage; now he is old. / His body like a withered pine, his mind like still water.
Thirteen: Subduing the Tiger
The fierce tiger in the hills shakes the woods with dread; / our Master's Way is high—of itself it tames and bows him.
Fourteen: Reading the Sutra
The true sutra has no words; cowhide covers the eyes. / Pierce it through—till then he cannot be bold.
Fifteen: At ease in Chan, a macaque offers fruit
Still and plain, with nothing in his breast. / The macaque is wildest of all, yet even it knows to yield.
Sixteen: Mending his robe in the morning sun. Seventeen: belly bared, facing each other, they only smile and look
The needle-and-thread craft is indeed fine and close; / but seen with a wide eye, it is still a strain.
Eighteen: Sitting upright in Chan samādhi
The place of great rest—calm and free. / Looking on with cool eyes, all of it is conjuring.
This monk is laughable—he cannot bear to stay idle. / Both hands grope and rub; no one knows why.
The Buddha's precepts and deportment are grave and dignified; / with fists flailing and feet kicking, it is most unseemly.
Dry sitting and wall-gazing are his own true calling; / stretching and yawning like this, one thinks his heart is dull.
Fierce courage has come to this: bow broken, arrows spent. / Still he clenches an empty fist—rage wasted in vain.
The kāṣāya is on his body, free from the first; / to add massage to it looks like conjuring.
Hands stretched out, feet drawn in, groping left and right. / There is one thing that was there all along—yet he cannot grasp it.
Begging in the street, he lost a thing. / He searches and cannot find it, beating his breast and stamping his feet.
He will not lie down to sleep, but goes to play with stones. / If he cracks his hand, he will have a heap of trouble.
Beating his back with a backward hand, he must have a pain in his spine. / The young feel nothing; in old age it grows heavy.
Upright as a lone pine—that is a monk's true model. / Carrying on like a child at play, what manner is this?
Both hands clasp his head—old age is doddering. / If not palsy, then it is deafness.
The Elder's countenance is most refined and grave, / yet his heels show—these little things fall short.
Waking from a doze, the dream not yet shaken off, / eyes wide open, he drives a peg into empty space.
Who is chasing him, with anger filling his belly? / Hurrying in a fluster, afraid of being caught.
He is unskilled at walking meditation; on level ground he stumbles. / Though he leaps up, the loss is already done.
Four limbs drawn in like fists, a hundred bones like cotton— / he must have met cold weather, frozen and starved.
May I ask the Elder how many years he has seen? / Just look at his two brows—few in the world have such.
He was steady to begin with, yet he seeks work for himself, / like a boat in the waves—whose fault is that?
One: A pair of sutras and incense in the censer, sitting upright and still
Sitting still, conditions forgotten, without thought or care. / Sutras and censer incense are idle furnishings.
Two: Reading the Sutra
Holding one scroll of sutra, his aim is to cover his eyes. / If he pierces the cowhide, he will patch the long with the short.
Three: Walking with his staff slung across his shoulder
His staff slung across, he walks alone, he steps alone. / Just go straight on—why look back?
Four: Leaning on his staff, gazing at the waterfall
Leaning on his staff, idly watching a thousand-fathom waterfall. / Ask where it comes from—he does not know the reason.
Five: Stroking a deer, sitting to watch butterflies
The deer has forgotten its wariness and comes to sit beside him. / The butterflies flutter on—his fevered dream is not yet broken.
Six: Holding the ruyi scepter, sitting with belly bared
Belly bared and slumped, having nothing at all. / A pity he has not forgotten the hand that holds the ruyi.
Seven: Walking with a sutra scroll in hand
Having entered liberation, with no hindrance and no tie, / this little thing in his hand becomes mere talk.
Eight: Sitting beneath peach blossoms, turning his head to read the sutra
Under the blossoms he looks closely—surely not for anything else: / he would have people know that emptiness itself is form.
Nine: Reaching into the bowl to scoop the moon
There is water in the bowl, and in the water a moon. / He reaches out to grab it—and in the end gets nothing.
Ten: Bowing to the distant sky
Bowing on level ground, with nothing before his eyes. / Do not take the void to be the Dharma-body Buddha.
The dragon among the clouds transforms at will. / Why subdue it, and turn it into conjuring?
Twelve: Stroking a tree and gazing at the spring
Alone he strokes a withered stump, quietly watching the flowing water. / Of all the idle folk in the world, none is idler than he.
Thirteen: Looking up at high mountains and flowing water
Flowing water and high mountains—few are those who understand. / Our Master has grasped it, beyond all expectation.
Fourteen: Leaning on his staff, walking at leisure
Leaning on his staff he strolls, stepping freely along. / In this world there are few such monks with nothing to do.
Fifteen: Riding a tiger
A fierce tiger is hard to tame; all who see it flee. / Our Master straddles it as if it were child's play.
Sixteen: Sitting to watch the moon in the water
Bright moon on the cold pool, its light shining through and through. / To plant a foot in this turns into mere dust.
Seventeen: Pointing at the sky with his finger
He points at the sky with his hand—what is there in the sky? / Though he points it out, it seems to air the family shame.
Eighteen: Holding his staff, sitting on a great rock
He has come to forgetting altogether, happy beyond compare. / The staff in his hand—why not put it down?
Also: Eulogy on the Golden-Line Painting of the Eighteen Elders Riding Beasts at Play

The three poisons are cleared away, birth and death no longer bind him; / thus he gains spiritual powers and sports at ease. / Fierce beasts and glaring dragons, each and every one is tamed; / he rides them as he pleases and lets them gallop where they will. / Because he himself has forgotten contrivance, creatures too forget him; / both are forgotten together, like fire entering fire. / He wanders through the ten directions, coming and going without hindrance; / those who do not know him are startled when they see. / This deceives only the foolish—it cannot escape the eye of wisdom. / Should he meet Vimalakīrti, he would surely be taken to task. / To give rise to false discrimination in the midst of emptiness— / even if it be gold dust, it is still a speck in the eye.
Eulogy on the Picture of the Sixteen Elders, the True-Being Arhats
About to go, yet not going, as if pondering something. / For whom does he ponder? Our Master himself knows.
His staff slung across, his bundle carried on his back, / suddenly he turns his head—just this is it.
Standing with a hollow ring of footsteps, gazing as if something were lost. / Lifting a hand toward the distant sky—who is it facing him?
Bones thin as firewood, robe loose as a sack. / Were he not forgetful of form, who could bear such a wrap?
The water in the bowl, the dragon in the sky, / the hand that seizes the clouds—another display of spiritual power.
Sitting there stiff and still, half resentful, half pondering. / The bowl's water is clear and calm—who is it that drops in a needle?
Drifting as if mad, startled as if angry. / Even if he is without intent, he still falls to watching and waiting.
A fierce tiger is easy to tame; a deluded mind is hard to unloose. / Were it not for our Master, it would nearly come to ruin.
Bones thin, spirit weary, his long brows a great burden. / All day he pushes at them, his arm aching and strengthless.
Shrinking from the cold, he pulls his robe about him, hugging his knees as if in thought. / He turns his head away—what is there to think about?
Things that are in emptiness contend with you for nothing. / To seek them without cause—can that be called sage?
Bending low, head bowed, palms joined toward the sky: / because he sees the Dharma-body, he pays homage to the true form.
His bamboo hat like emptiness, his staff like a dragon, / he roams beyond all things and in an instant sheds the cage.
The vase holds nothing to begin with—where do these strange lights come from? / He lets them out and gathers them himself, with no one to tend them.
Both hands wrestle empty air, both feet hurry along. / Though he bustles for another, he displays his own shame.
Hooded under his patchwork quilt, he steals a cold-eyed glance. / Where the incense smoke rises—just that is it.
Eulogy on the Fourteen Elders
One: Hooded in a patchwork robe, palms joined, head bowed
Hooded in one robe, he sits through all conditions. / Palms joined and head bowed, thus he receives in faith.
Two: Subduing a lion, holding its cub, urging it to spring
The lion springs with mighty power. / To snatch its cub—will it not leap back?
Three: Planting his staff, raising his fist, walking alone, stepping alone
One staff props up the sky; two fists grip bone. / His Dharma power is boundless—he chants Namo Buddha.
Four: Three men sitting together, as if preaching the Dharma
Speaking without a tongue, hearing without ears. / The sound of Dharma is like thunder—no one will believe it.
Five: Sitting upright in silence
Delusions from kalpas past are unseen in the bustle; / but when he sits in silence, they all appear at once.
Six: Chan Samādhi
His robe is like emptiness, his spine like iron. / Sitting through the ten directions, he ends up with a branded brow.
Seven: Lifting the Bowl
Both hands lift the bowl, offering up the whole tray. / Look closely, all of you—what is there inside?
Eight: Great belly, bare midriff
A great belly is hard to hide; long feet are hard to draw in. / You have taken a dislike of your own—it is no fault of mine.
Nine: Reading the sutra under the moon
The moonlight is bright as day; old eyes are not sleepy. / He rises to recite the sutra, taking it to relieve his gloom.
Ten: Spreading his sitting cloth and taking his seat
